title: Responsive Design
summary: Responsive design is layout that adapts to the space it's given, not the device it guesses it's on. Learn mobile-first media queries, fluid units, container queries, and where clamp() replaces both.

slides.markdown:
"Responsive" originally meant "works on a phone and a desktop." That framing is already outdated — a single phone can host a full-screen browser tab and a half-screen split-view app, and a desktop window gets resized constantly. The real target isn't a device category, it's an **unknown, changing viewport size**.

This topic covers the toolkit for that: media queries that key off content breakpoints rather than named devices, fluid units that scale instead of stepping, and container queries — the newer piece that responds to a component's own box, not the whole viewport.

The throughline across all of it: stop asking "is this a phone?" and start asking "how much space do I actually have right now?"

slides.sectionTitle: Picking breakpoints from content, not devices
slides.markdown:
A breakpoint list like "iPhone SE, iPhone 14, iPad, laptop, 4K monitor" is a losing strategy — it chases a moving target of device dimensions that changes every year, and it misses split-screen, foldables, and browser zoom entirely.

The durable approach: resize the component itself and add a breakpoint **exactly where the content starts to look wrong** — text lines get too long, a three-column layout gets cramped, a nav bar starts wrapping ugly. That's a content-based breakpoint, and it's specific to the component, not the whole site.

Most real projects still converge on a small shared set (something like 480px, 768px, 1024px, 1280px) for consistency across components, but the set is derived by testing content at real widths, not copied from a device spec sheet.

slides.subTitle: Picking the right unit
slides.markdown:
| Unit | Relative to | Best for |
|---|---|---|
| `%` | the parent element's size | widths inside a fluid container |
| `vw`/`vh` | the viewport | full-bleed sections, hero heights |
| `rem` | the root `<html>` font-size | spacing and font sizes that should scale with user zoom/preferences |
| `px` | nothing — absolute | borders, shadows, fine details that shouldn't scale |

The common mistake is using `vw` alone for font-size: it scales smoothly with viewport width but ignores the user's browser zoom and OS text-size settings, which is an accessibility problem — a user who bumped their default font size for readability gets overridden. `rem` respects that because it's tied to the root font-size, which browser zoom and OS settings both affect.

`px` isn't "wrong," it's just non-scaling by design — correct for a 1px border, wrong for body text.

slides.subTitle: Styling by parent size, not viewport size

slides.markdown:
Take a single card component with an image, a title, and a description, and drop it into three containers of different widths using the container-query rule from the previous slide.

At a wide container (above the 400px threshold), the card lays out horizontally — image on the left, text on the right. At a narrow container (below 400px, in a tight sidebar or a mobile split-view), the same component stacks the image above the text. No viewport media query fires here at all — the exact same viewport width could produce either layout depending purely on which container the card happens to sit in.

slides.sectionTitle: Responsive images: srcset, sizes, and picture
slides.markdown: Shipping one image file to every viewport wastes bandwidth on small screens and looks soft on high-density ones. `srcset` + `sizes` let the browser choose: ```html ``` `srcset` lists candidate files with their real widths; `sizes` tells the browser how wide the image will actually render at each breakpoint, so it can pick the smallest candidate that's still sharp enough — all without JavaScript. `` goes further for **art direction** — swapping to a genuinely different crop, not just a different resolution: ```html ``` Use `srcset`/`sizes` for "same image, different resolution"; use `` when the crop or aspect ratio itself needs to change.

slides.subTitle: The unclamped vw pitfall
slides.markdown:
`font-size: 3vw` looks fine on a designer's 1440px laptop and becomes unreadable on a 320px phone (about 9.6px) or comically large on a 3440px ultrawide monitor (about 103px). Pure viewport units have no built-in floor or ceiling — they scale linearly forever in both directions, past the point where the design still makes sense.

This is a real accessibility problem too, not just an aesthetic one: text that shrinks below roughly 12–14px effective size on a small viewport fails basic readability, independent of any zoom the user applies afterward.

The fix is always the same: wrap the `vw` value in `clamp()` with sane min/max bounds, or fall back to a fixed size inside a `min-width` media query if the codebase predates `clamp()` support. "I used `vw` for scaling" is an incomplete answer in an interview; "I used `vw` inside `clamp()` so it can't go below 1rem or above 3rem" is the complete one.

slides.sectionTitle: Making a card component responsive, live
slides.markdown:
"Make this card responsive" as a live exercise is really testing whether you reach for the right tool at each layer, not whether you know one trick. A strong pass through it touches most of this topic in order:

1. Lay out the card content with flexbox or grid so it isn't dependent on a fixed width to begin with.
2. Use `clamp()` for the card's padding and heading size so it scales smoothly without a media query.
3. Add a content-based breakpoint (not a device one) where the card's internal layout genuinely needs to change — say, switching from a horizontal to stacked image/text arrangement.
4. If the card is meant to be a reusable component dropped into sidebars, modals, and full-width sections alike, reach for a **container query** instead of a viewport media query, since the card's context — not the viewport — is what actually varies.

Naming which of these four tools solves which sub-problem, out loud, is what separates a fluent answer from one that just adds `@media` rules until it looks right on the interviewer's monitor.

Resizing a browser window is a starting point, not a test plan. A few habits catch what window-dragging misses:

- **Test at the actual breakpoint boundaries**, not just "looks fine at a few random widths" — off-by-one pixel bugs live exactly at a `min-width` threshold.
- **Zoom the browser to 200%** — this simulates both low-vision users and, differently, a very small effective viewport, and it's the fastest way to catch unclamped `vw` text.
- **Check landscape on mobile emulation**, not just portrait — a fixed-height hero section that was fine in portrait often eats the whole screen in landscape.
- **Throttle the network** when testing `srcset`/`sizes` — the point of responsive images is invisible on a fast connection and very visible on a slow one.

Devtools' device toolbar is useful for a first pass, but it emulates viewport size, not real device rendering quirks — a final check on at least one real phone and one real tablet catches things emulation doesn't.
